cards.q: What does `javac` produce, and what runs it?
cards.a:
Bytecode in `.class` files, which the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs

`javac` turns source code into bytecode in `.class` files: instructions for the JVM, not for any real processor, which is why the same file runs on any system.
cards.lessonTitle: Java and the JDK: Your First Program

cards.q: What must the file containing `public class Greeter` be called?
cards.a:
`Greeter.java`

A public class must be in a file with exactly its name plus `.java`. Java is case-sensitive, so `greeter.java` does not match, and `Greeter.class` is what the compiler produces.
cards.lessonTitle: Java and the JDK: Your First Program

cards.q: Which line starts a Java program?
cards.a:
`public static void main(String[] args) {`

The JVM starts by calling the main method. The class only holds it.
cards.lessonTitle: Java and the JDK: Your First Program

cards.q: Why does `long population = 8100000000;` not compile?
cards.a:
The number is an `int` literal and too big for `int`; write `8_100_000_000L`

A whole number with no suffix is an `int` literal, and 8 100 000 000 does not fit in an int even though it fits in a long. The `L` suffix makes it a long literal; underscores only help readability.

cards.q: What is `(int) 7.9`?
cards.a:
7

Casting a double to int cuts off the fraction; it does not round. The cast is exactly what makes this narrowing conversion allowed.

cards.q: What does `int x = Integer.MAX_VALUE; x = x + 1;` leave in `x`?
cards.a:
`Integer.MIN_VALUE`, -2147483648

int arithmetic wraps around silently on overflow; 2147483648 does not fit in an int. `Math.addExact` throws an exception instead.

cards.q: What are `23 / 4` and `23 % 4` when both are ints?
cards.a:
5 and 3

int / int is integer division, so the fraction is cut off: 23 / 4 is 5. The remainder 23 % 4 is 3, because 4 * 5 = 20 and 23 - 20 = 3.

cards.q: What does `"Sum: " + 1 + 2` produce?
cards.a:
`"Sum: 12"`

`+` works left to right, and once a String is involved it joins text: "Sum: " + 1 is "Sum: 1", then + 2 gives "Sum: 12". Write `"Sum: " + (1 + 2)` to get Sum: 3.

cards.q: What does `7 / 2 * 2.0` evaluate to?
cards.a:
6.0

7 / 2 is integer division (3) and happens first; 3 * 2.0 is the double 6.0.

cards.q: Why can `a == b` print `false` for two strings that both contain "hello"?
cards.a:
`==` compares references, and they are two different objects; `equals` compares the text

On objects, `==` asks "is this the same object?". Two strings with the same text can be different objects, so compare text with `equals` (`equalsIgnoreCase` is the one that ignores case).

cards.q: What is `"programming".substring(3, 7)`?
cards.a:
`"gram"`

The characters from index 3 up to, but not including, index 7: g, r, a, m. Indexes start at 0, and the end index is excluded.

cards.q: After `int n = in.nextInt(); String s = in.nextLine();` with the input "5" then "Ada" on the next line, what is `s`?
cards.a:
`""` (the empty rest of the line after 5)

`nextInt` reads the number but leaves the line break; `nextLine` then reads the empty rest of that line, not "Ada".

cards.q: What happens in a classic (colon) switch when a case has no `break`?
cards.a:
Execution falls through into the next case's statements

In the classic form, cases fall through until a `break` (or the end of the switch), and the compiler allows it. The arrow form never falls through.

cards.q: What does `break outer;` do inside two nested loops, where the outer loop is labelled `outer:`?
cards.a:
Leaves the loop labelled `outer`, including the loop nested inside it

A labelled break leaves the labelled loop and everything nested in it. Skipping to the next round of the outer loop would be `continue outer;`.

cards.q: How many times does `for (int i = 10; i > 0; i -= 4)` run its body?
cards.a:
3

i takes the values 10, 6 and 2; the next value, -2, fails the test `i > 0`.

cards.q: A method sets its `int` parameter to 5. Has the caller's variable changed afterwards?
cards.a:
No: Java passed a copy of the value

Java always passes copies of values. Changing the copy inside the method leaves the caller's variable as it was; returning a value only helps if the caller assigns it.

cards.q: Can a method change the contents of an array passed to it?
cards.a:
Yes: it gets a copy of the reference, which points to the same array

The method receives a copy of the reference, not a copy of the array, so `values[0] = 9` changes the caller's array. Making the parameter point to a new array does not affect the caller, though.

cards.q: Which pair of methods can NOT both exist in one class?
cards.a:
`int f(int x)` and `double f(int x)`

Overloads must differ in their parameter lists; a different return type alone is not enough.

cards.q: What are the valid indexes of an array of length 5?
cards.a:
0 to 4

Indexes start at 0, so the last one is `length - 1`, which is 4. Index 5 throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

cards.q: Why does `System.out.println(array)` not show the values?
cards.a:
Arrays have no readable `toString`; use `Arrays.toString(array)`

Printing an array directly gives its type and an identity code, something like `[I@1b6d3586`. `Arrays.toString` (or `Arrays.deepToString` for 2D arrays) shows the contents.

cards.q: After `int[] b = a; b[0] = 5;`, what is `a[0]`?
cards.a:
5

`a` and `b` refer to the same array, so a change through one is seen through the other; use `a.clone()` for a copy.

cards.q: Why can you not write `List<int>`?
cards.a:
Generic collections hold objects only; use the wrapper type `List<Integer>`

Collections hold objects, not primitives. Each primitive has a wrapper class, and autoboxing converts between `int` and `Integer` for you.

cards.q: On a `List<Integer>`, what does `list.remove(1)` remove?
cards.a:
The item at index 1

With an `int` argument, `remove` picks the by-index version. To remove the value 1, call `list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))`.

cards.q: What happens when you call `add` on `List.of(1, 2)`?
cards.a:
`UnsupportedOperationException` is thrown

`List.of` returns an unmodifiable list. It compiles, because the type is still `List`, but changing it fails at run time; copy it with `new ArrayList<>(...)` to get a list you can change.

cards.q: What two parts does every recursive method need?
cards.a:
A base case, and a recursive case that moves toward it

The base case stops the recursion; the recursive case calls the method on a smaller problem so the base case is eventually reached. Without that, the calls pile up until `StackOverflowError`.

cards.q: Why is the plain recursive Fibonacci slow?
cards.a:
It recomputes the same smaller values again and again

`fib(n)` calls `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`, which compute the same smaller values again and again, so the number of calls grows exponentially (roughly 1.6ⁿ). Memoization stores each answer once.

cards.q: What does `f(3)` print for `static void f(int n) { if (n == 0) return; f(n - 1); System.out.print(n); }`?
cards.a:
123

The print happens after the recursive call returns, so the deepest call (n = 1) prints first; `f(0)` returns without printing.

cards.q: Why build a long string in a loop with `StringBuilder` rather than `+=`?
cards.a:
Strings are immutable, so `+=` copies the whole string every time; `StringBuilder` appends in place

Each `+=` creates a brand-new string and copies everything so far, which is quadratic in a loop. A `StringBuilder` is a mutable buffer you append to.

cards.q: What is `'7' - '0'`, and why?
cards.a:
7, because the codes of `'0'` to `'9'` are consecutive

Arithmetic on chars works on their codes, and the digit codes are in order. `'7'` is 55 and `'0'` is 48, so the difference is the digit's value, 7.

cards.q: What does `"a1b22c333".split("\\d+")` return?
cards.a:
`["a", "b", "c"]`

The runs of digits are the separators and are not kept; the trailing empty piece after "333" is dropped.

cards.q: What is the difference between a class and an object?
cards.a:
A class is the blueprint; an object is one instance made from it with `new`, with its own field values

The class describes the fields and methods. Each `new` creates a separate instance, and every instance has its own copy of the fields.

cards.q: What does `this.name = name;` do in a constructor?
cards.a:
Copies the parameter `name` into the object's field called `name`

`this` is the object being constructed, so `this.name` is its field, while plain `name` is the parameter that hides it.

cards.q: `Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = new Point(1, 2);` Without an `equals` override, what is `a.equals(b)`?
cards.a:
false

`Object.equals` compares references unless the class overrides it, and `a` and `b` are two different objects.

cards.q: Why make fields `private` instead of `public`?
cards.a:
So only the class's own methods can change them and keep the object valid

Callers then have to go through methods like `deposit`, which can refuse nonsense values. Subclasses cannot see private fields either.

cards.q: Can a `static` method use `this`?
cards.a:
No: a static method runs without any object

A static method belongs to the class, so it has no `this`; it can use only static fields, other static methods and its parameters.

cards.q: A class has `private static int count = 0;` and its constructor does `count++`. After creating 3 objects, what is `count`?
cards.a:
3, shared by all objects

A static field is a single variable shared by the whole class, so every constructor call adds to the same one.

cards.q: `Employee e = new Manager(...); e.monthlyCost();` Which version of the overridden method runs?
cards.a:
`Manager`'s, because the actual object's class decides at run time

Dynamic dispatch picks the method of the object's real class when the program runs. The variable's type only decides which methods you may call.

cards.q: Why must `equals` and `hashCode` be overridden together?
cards.a:
Hash-based collections look up by hash code before calling `equals`

The rule is that equal objects must have equal hash codes, because a `HashSet` or `HashMap` only calls `equals` on objects in the same hash bucket. Override only `equals`, and a `HashSet` can hold two "equal" books. The compiler does not check this.

cards.q: A subclass constructor does not call `super(...)`. What happens?
cards.a:
Java calls the superclass's no-argument constructor for it

`super()` is called implicitly. If the superclass has no no-argument constructor, that is a compile error.

cards.q: Can you create an object of an abstract class with `new`?
cards.a:
No; only of concrete subclasses that implement every abstract method

`new Shape(...)` does not compile when `Shape` is abstract. An abstract class can still have constructors, which its subclasses call with `super(...)`.

cards.q: Why must a method that implements an interface method be `public`?
cards.a:
Interface methods are implicitly public, and an implementation may not reduce visibility

Leaving out `public` gives the method package access, which is narrower than the interface's public method, so the compiler refuses it.

cards.q: A class wants to be sortable with `Collections.sort`. What should it implement?
cards.a:
`Comparable<T>`

`Comparable` defines the natural order through `compareTo`, which `Collections.sort` uses. `Iterable` only makes it usable in an enhanced for.

cards.q: What does `record Point(int x, int y) { }` give you?
cards.a:
Private final fields, a constructor, accessors `x()` and `y()`, and value-based `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`

A record generates all of that from its components. The accessors are named after the components (`x()`, not `getX()`), and the fields are final, so a record is immutable.

cards.q: Why can a `switch` over a sealed interface leave out `default`?
cards.a:
The compiler knows every permitted subtype, so it can check that all are handled

The `permits` list names every possible subtype, so the compiler can prove the switch is exhaustive, and it stops compiling when a new subtype is added but not handled.

cards.q: Which is the best type for the four card suits?
cards.a:
An enum `Suit { HEARTS, DIAMONDS, CLUBS, SPADES }`

An enum gives a fixed, type-checked set of values, and a `switch` over it can be checked for completeness. Ints, strings and records all allow invalid values.

cards.q: Why can't you pass a `List<Integer>` where a `List<Number>` is expected?
cards.a:
The method could add a `Double` through the `List<Number>` type, breaking the list of integers

`Integer` is a `Number`, but a list of integers is not a list of numbers: a `List<Number>` accepts any number. Use `List<? extends Number>` for a parameter you only read from.

cards.q: Which parameter type lets a method add `Integer`s to a list of `Integer`s, `Number`s or `Object`s?
cards.a:
`List<? super Integer>`

PECS: a consumer that you write into takes `? super T`. `? extends Integer` only lets you read, and `List<Integer>` accepts only lists of exactly `Integer`.

cards.q: What does `<T extends Comparable<T>>` allow inside the method?
cards.a:
Calling `compareTo` on values of type `T`

The bound guarantees every `T` has `compareTo`. `new T()` is still impossible because of type erasure.

cards.q: Which set keeps its items sorted?
cards.a:
`TreeSet`

`TreeSet` keeps its items in sorted order. `HashSet` has no useful order, and `LinkedHashSet` keeps the order the items were first added.

cards.q: What does `map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)` do?
cards.a:
Puts 1 if `word` is not yet a key, otherwise adds 1 to its current value

`merge` stores the given value for a new key; for an existing key it combines the old value and the given one with the function, here `Integer::sum`. That makes it the one-line way to count.

cards.q: A class overrides `equals` but not `hashCode`, and two equal objects are added to a `HashSet`. How many items does the set hold?
cards.a:
Probably 2, because their hash codes differ

`HashSet` looks in the bucket for the hash code first; with different hash codes, `equals` is never even asked.

cards.q: When do you use a `Comparator` instead of `Comparable`?
cards.a:
When you need an order other than the class's natural order, or the class has none you can add

`Comparable` gives one natural order, written inside the class. A `Comparator` is kept outside, so a class can be sorted many ways, including classes you cannot change.

cards.q: Why is `return a.score - b.score;` a risky `compareTo`?
cards.a:
The subtraction can overflow for large values and give the wrong sign

Any negative, zero or positive result is allowed, but `Integer.MIN_VALUE - 1` overflows to a large positive number. `Integer.compare` cannot overflow.

cards.q: A list of people is sorted by name, then sorted again by age (a stable sort). How are people of the same age ordered?
cards.a:
By name

A stable sort keeps the earlier (name) order among items that compare equal on age.

cards.q: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?
cards.a:
Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with `throws`; unchecked ones (`RuntimeException` subclasses) need not be

Both kinds are thrown at run time and both can be caught. The difference is that the compiler forces you to handle or declare checked ones like `IOException`.

cards.q: What does try-with-resources guarantee?
cards.a:
Its resources are closed when the block ends, even by an exception

It works with any `AutoCloseable` and closes the resources in reverse order of opening, whether the block ends normally or not; exceptions still travel on to a `catch` or the caller.

cards.q: A method calls `Files.readString(path)`, which throws `IOException`, and does not catch it. What must its signature include?
cards.a:
`throws IOException`

`IOException` is checked: it must be caught or declared with `throws` in the method signature.

cards.q: Why read a large file with `Files.lines` or a `BufferedReader` instead of `readAllLines`?
cards.a:
They read one line at a time instead of loading the whole file into memory

`readAllLines` returns a `List` holding every line at once, which can use a lot of memory for a big file. Close `Files.lines` and readers with try-with-resources.

cards.q: Why must a `BufferedWriter` be closed?
cards.a:
Writing is buffered; closing flushes the remaining data to the file and releases it

Text goes into a buffer first and only reaches the file when the buffer is flushed. Without `close` (or try-with-resources), the last part can be lost.

cards.q: Which builds the path to `data/2026/report.csv` portably?
cards.a:
`Path.of("data", "2026", "report.csv")`

`Path.of` joins the parts with the right separator for the system; gluing strings hard-codes one separator.

cards.q: What is the Big O of `5n² + 100n + 7`?
cards.a:
O(n²)

The fastest-growing term dominates and constant factors are dropped, so only `n²` is left.

cards.q: Why is a loop over `n` words that calls `contains` on an `ArrayList` inside it usually O(n²)?
cards.a:
`contains` scans the list, O(n), and it runs once per iteration of an O(n) loop

A method call costs what the method costs: an O(n) scan inside an O(n) loop multiplies to O(n²). A `HashSet` makes each `contains` O(1) on average.

cards.q: A loop does `for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2)`. How many times does it run?
cards.a:
about log₂ n

`i` doubles each time, so it reaches `n` after about log₂ n steps.

cards.q: Quicksort is O(n log n) on average. What is its worst case?
cards.a:
O(n²)

Quicksort can degrade to O(n²) when its pivots split the data badly; merge sort is the one that is O(n log n) always.

cards.q: Why is binary search O(log n)?
cards.a:
Each comparison halves the range that can still contain the target

Halving the range each step means a range of n items is down to one after about log₂ n comparisons.

cards.q: Merge sort is stable. What does that mean, and what in the merge makes it so?
cards.a:
Equal items keep their original order; taking from the left half when `a[i] <= a[j]` does that

On a tie the merge takes the item from the left half, which came first in the original. With `<` instead of `<=` equal items could swap places.

cards.q: Which sort is O(n log n) even in the worst case?
cards.a:
Merge sort

Merge sort always splits evenly; quicksort can degrade to O(n²) with bad pivots.

cards.q: Why is `get(i)` O(n) for a linked list?
cards.a:
There is no index: it must follow `i` links from the head

Nodes are not stored next to each other, so the only way to item `i` is to follow `next` links one at a time.

cards.q: Besides a node in the middle, which cases must `remove` handle?
cards.a:
The head, the tail, a one-node list, and a value that is not there

Most linked-list bugs live at the edges: the head has no predecessor, the tail reference must move back, and a missing value must leave the list untouched.

cards.q: In the `reverse` method, what would happen without `Node<T> next = cur.next;` at the start of the loop?
cards.a:
The rest of the list would be lost after `cur.next = prev`

The original next link must be saved before it is overwritten; otherwise there is no way to reach the following node.

cards.q: Why does doubling the capacity make `ArrayList.add` amortised O(1)?
cards.a:
Copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., n, which add up to less than 2n copies for n adds

A single resize is O(n), but they are so rare that the total copying stays below 2n, a constant amount per add on average.

cards.q: What happens to a hash table's speed if every key has the same `hashCode`?
cards.a:
All entries share one bucket, so lookups scan a list: O(n)

`hashCode` picks the bucket; if they are all equal, one bucket holds everything and resizing does not help, because the keys still all land together.

cards.q: Evaluating the postfix expression `6 2 /` with the stack method above gives:
cards.a:
3

`b = 2` is popped first, then `a = 6`, and `a / b = 3`; the order matters for `-` and `/`.

cards.q: What does an in-order traversal of a BST produce?
cards.a:
The keys in sorted order

In-order visits left, node, right; with smaller keys on the left that is ascending order. Root first is pre-order, level by level is level-order.

cards.q: Why can inserting 1, 2, 3, ..., n into a plain BST be slow?
cards.a:
Each key becomes the right child of the last, so the tree is a chain

The chain has height about n, so operations become O(n): a plain BST does not rebalance, and sorted input turns it into a linked list. Self-balancing trees like `TreeMap` keep the height O(log n).

cards.q: Deleting a node with two children replaces its key with:
cards.a:
the smallest key in its right subtree

The in-order successor keeps the BST property; the largest key in the left subtree would also work.

cards.q: What makes an interface usable with a lambda?
cards.a:
It has exactly one abstract method

Any interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface. `@FunctionalInterface` only asks the compiler to check that; it is not required.

cards.q: Which functional interface fits "takes a `String`, returns true or false"?
cards.a:
`Predicate<String>`

`Predicate<T>` has `boolean test(T t)`. A `Consumer` returns nothing and a `Supplier` takes no input.

cards.q: What is `f.andThen(g).apply(x)` the same as?
cards.a:
`g.apply(f.apply(x))`

`andThen` runs `f` first, then `g` on its result; `compose` is the other order.

cards.q: What happens if a stream pipeline has no terminal operation?
cards.a:
Nothing runs: intermediate operations are lazy

Intermediate operations only describe the work; it happens when a terminal operation such as `toList()` or `count()` asks for results.

cards.q: What does `Collectors.groupingBy(Person::city, Collectors.counting())` produce?
cards.a:
A `Map` from each city to the number of people in it

The second collector decides what each group becomes: `counting()` turns each city's people into a `Long` count. Without it, each group would be a `List<Person>`.

cards.q: What is `Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).map(n -> n * 10).toList()`?
cards.a:
`[20, 40]`

The even numbers 2 and 4 remain and are multiplied by 10.

cards.q: What is the difference between `orElse` and `orElseGet`?
cards.a:
`orElse` always evaluates its default; `orElseGet` only calls its supplier when the `Optional` is empty

The argument of `orElse` is computed before the call even when a value is present; `orElseGet` takes a `Supplier` and runs it only if needed.

cards.q: Where should `Optional` be used?
cards.a:
As the return type of methods that may have no result

`Optional` is meant for return types that may be "nothing"; for fields and parameters it only adds clutter.

cards.q: What does `Optional.of(" ").map(String::trim).filter(s -> !s.isEmpty()).orElse("blank")` return?
cards.a:
`"blank"`

`trim` gives `""`, the filter removes it, and `orElse` supplies the default.

cards.q: Why can two threads incrementing the same `int` with `count++` lose updates?
cards.a:
`count++` is a read, an add and a write, and the threads' steps can interleave

Two threads can both read the old value, both add one, and both write it back: one increment is lost. `synchronized` or `AtomicInteger` prevents that.

cards.q: What does `future.get()` do?
cards.a:
Waits until the task has finished and returns its result, or throws if the task failed

`get()` blocks the calling thread until the result is ready; submitting the task to the executor is what starts it.

cards.q: Thread A locks X then Y; thread B locks Y then X. What can happen?
cards.a:
A deadlock, with both threads waiting forever

Each holds the lock the other needs; taking locks in a fixed order prevents it.

cards.q: In a Maven or Gradle project, which file holds the class `com.example.planner.model.Event`?
cards.a:
`src/main/java/com/example/planner/model/Event.java`

Each part of the package name is a folder under `src/main/java`; `src/test/java` is for the tests.

cards.q: Which members of a class can a class in another package use?
cards.a:
Only `public` ones (and `protected` ones from subclasses)

Members without a modifier are package-private: visible only inside their own package. That is how a package hides its helpers.

cards.q: What does `mvn test` do?
cards.a:
Compiles the code and runs the unit tests under `src/test/java`

Maven's test phase runs after compile and runs the JUnit tests.

cards.q: When should a nested class be `static`?
cards.a:
Whenever it does not need an object of the outer class

That is most of the time. A `static` nested class has no hidden reference to an outer object, so it is simpler and does not keep the outer object alive. Its methods can still be ordinary instance methods.

cards.q: What does "effectively final" mean for a local variable?
cards.a:
It is never assigned again after it is first set

The `final` keyword is not needed: any local variable that is never reassigned counts, and only those can be captured by a lambda or local class.

cards.q: What does an inner (non-static) class object always hold?
cards.a:
a reference to an object of the outer class

That hidden reference is how inner classes reach the outer object's fields, and why they keep it alive.

cards.q: Why must equal objects have equal hash codes?
cards.a:
Hash collections look in the bucket that `hashCode` picks

`HashSet` and `HashMap` pick a bucket by `hashCode` and only then ask `equals`, so an equal object with another hash code is looked for in the wrong bucket and never found. Unequal objects may share a hash code; equal ones must.
cards.lessonTitle: equals, hashCode and the Object Contract

cards.q: Two different people compare as 0 in a `TreeSet`'s comparator. What happens?
cards.a:
The set treats them as the same element and keeps only one

`TreeSet` uses the comparator instead of `equals`: comparing as 0 means "already there". Adding `thenComparing(Person::name)` keeps both.
cards.lessonTitle: equals, hashCode and the Object Contract

cards.q: A class overrides `equals` but not `hashCode`. Which collection is most likely to misbehave?
cards.a:
`HashSet`

`HashSet` uses `hashCode` to find elements; `ArrayList.contains` uses `equals` alone.
cards.lessonTitle: equals, hashCode and the Object Contract

cards.q: Why must an annotation read by reflection have `@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)`?
cards.a:
Other retention policies drop the annotation before the program runs, so reflection never sees it

`SOURCE` annotations vanish after compiling and `CLASS` ones are in the class file but invisible at run time; only `RUNTIME` ones reach `getAnnotation`.

cards.q: A method called through `Method.invoke` throws `IllegalStateException`. What does the caller receive?
cards.a:
An `InvocationTargetException` whose `getCause()` is the `IllegalStateException`

`invoke` wraps whatever the method throws; unwrap it with `getCause()` to get the real exception.

cards.q: Which returns a class's private methods too?
cards.a:
`getDeclaredMethods()`

`getDeclaredMethods` lists every method declared in the class itself, whatever its access; `getMethods` lists only public ones, inherited ones included.

cards.q: Which type should a server store for "when did this happen"?
cards.a:
An `Instant`, a moment that is the same everywhere

An `Instant` means the same moment for everyone; a zone is applied only when showing it to a person. A `LocalDateTime` has no zone, so it does not pin down a moment.

cards.q: Why does `LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31).plusMonths(1)` give 28 February?
cards.a:
February has no 31st, so the result is clamped to the last valid day of the month

`plusMonths` moves the month and keeps the day if it can; when the day does not exist, it uses the month's last day.

cards.q: What is the difference between `Duration.ofDays(1)` and `Period.ofDays(1)`?
cards.a:
`Duration` is always 24 hours; `Period` is a calendar day, which can be 23 or 25

`Duration` measures exact time; `Period` counts calendar units, so across a daylight-saving change one day can be 23 or 25 hours.

cards.q: What does `in.read()` return at the end of a stream?
cards.a:
`-1`

Real bytes come back as 0 to 255, so `-1` cannot be confused with data. `0` is a perfectly valid byte. (`DataInputStream`'s `readInt` and friends are the ones that throw `EOFException`.)

cards.q: Why wrap a `FileOutputStream` in a `BufferedOutputStream`?
cards.a:
So many small writes reach the disk as a few large blocks

The buffer gathers small writes in memory, which is much faster. Each wrapper adds one ability: buffering adds speed. Compression is `GZIPOutputStream`, and closing is the job of `try` with resources.

cards.q: How is the int `0x0A0B0C0D` laid out in little-endian order?
cards.a:
`0D 0C 0B 0A`

Little-endian puts the lowest byte first.

cards.q: What is the difference between `matches()` and `find()`?
cards.a:
`matches()` must match the whole text; `find()` looks for the next place the pattern occurs anywhere

Use `matches()` to validate a whole string and `find()` to search inside one. `lookingAt()` is the one that matches only at the start.

cards.q: Why is `"1.2.3".split(".")` an empty array?
cards.a:
`.` means "any character", so every character is a separator

The argument of `split` is a regex; escape the dot as `"\\."` to split on a literal dot. Trailing empty parts are dropped, which leaves nothing.

cards.q: How is the regex `\d+` written in a Java string literal?
cards.a:
`"\\d+"`

Java strings use backslash for their own escapes, so each regex backslash is doubled.

cards.q: When do you use `thenCompose` rather than `thenApply`?
cards.a:
When the next step itself returns a `CompletableFuture`

`thenCompose` flattens the result, like `flatMap`; `thenApply` would give a future of a future. Combining two independent futures is `thenCombine`.

cards.q: Why are virtual threads good for a server handling many requests?
cards.a:
Each request can block in its own thread, and waiting ones cost almost nothing

A waiting virtual thread gives up its carrier thread, so many thousands can wait at once. They help with waiting, not with CPU-heavy work.

cards.q: A stage throws an exception. What happens to the `thenApply` steps after it?
cards.a:
they are skipped until an `exceptionally` or `handle` step

The future completes exceptionally; later transformation steps are skipped, and recovery steps see the error.

cards.q: What does `groupingBy(Sale::region, counting())` give?
cards.a:
A map from each region to the number of sales in it

The downstream `counting()` turns each group into a `Long`. Without a downstream collector, each group would be a `List<Sale>`.

cards.q: When does `toMap` throw, and how do you prevent it?
cards.a:
When two items produce the same key; pass a merge function as the third argument

`toMap(keyFn, valueFn)` throws `IllegalStateException` on a duplicate key; the merge function decides which value to keep, or how to combine them.

cards.q: Which collector always gives a map with exactly the keys `true` and `false`?
cards.a:
`partitioningBy(x -> x > 0)`

`partitioningBy` always has both keys; `groupingBy` only has keys that occur.

cards.q: Why is `new BigDecimal(0.1)` a mistake?
cards.a:
The double `0.1` is already slightly wrong in binary, and this constructor copies that exact wrong value

The result has dozens of digits of binary error. Use `new BigDecimal("0.1")` or `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)`.

cards.q: What does `Math.addExact` do that `+` does not?
cards.a:
It throws an `ArithmeticException` when the result does not fit

`+` on `int` wraps past 2,147,483,647 to a negative number with no error; `addExact` refuses.

cards.q: `new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"))` is...
cards.a:
`false`, because the scales differ

`equals` compares value and scale; `compareTo` compares only the value.

cards.q: Why format numbers for a file with `Locale.ROOT`?
cards.a:
So every computer writes the same decimal point and no grouping

Then the file can be read back anywhere. Without a locale, `String.format` uses the computer's default, so a German machine would write `3,50`, which `Double.parseDouble` cannot read back.

cards.q: Why might `"😀".length()` be 2?
cards.a:
`length()` counts UTF-16 code units, and the emoji needs two of them (a surrogate pair)

Most characters fit in one `char`, but emoji and some rare scripts need two; `codePointCount` counts real characters. (In UTF-8 the emoji is four bytes.)

cards.q: Which format prints 3.14 padded with zeros to width 8?
cards.a:
`"%08.2f"`

The `0` flag pads with zeros, 8 is the width, and `.2` gives two decimals: `00003.14`. `"%8.2f"` pads with spaces instead.
